title: Critical dynamics of a scalar field near four spatial dimensions
abstract: The critical dynamics of a non-conserved order parameter is generally expected to become overdamped at long distances, even when propagating modes occur at microscopic or intermediate scales. We investigate the critical dynamics of a scalar field theory in thermal equilibrium which, in addition to local friction and noise, also contains a time-dependent second-order kinetic term. We show how to build a supersymmetric field-theory formulation. Using a two-loop expansion about four spatial dimensions, we show that the propagating and strictly overdamped limits share the same static Gaussian and Wilson-Fisher fixed points but realize distinct dynamical scaling regimes. The overdamped limit reproduces Model A. On the surface where local friction and noise vanish, the theory instead supports an interacting propagating fixed point whose dynamic exponent receives corrections at two loops. We demonstrate that coarse-graining does not generate a local dissipative operator on this surface, which therefore remains invariant under the RG flow. Local dissipation is nevertheless relevant at the propagating fixed point: an arbitrarily small equilibrium friction-noise perturbation drives the flow away from propagating scaling. Propagating critical dynamics thus defines a consistent but fine-tuned regime that is unstable to local equilibrium dissipation.
summary: This paper analyzes the critical dynamics of a scalar field near four dimensions, focusing on how inertia and dissipation compete. Using supersymmetric field theory and RG methods, the authors demonstrate that while different dynamic limits exist, the propagating regime is inherently unstable when subjected to local equilibrium dissipation. This highlights the fine-tuned nature required for sustained wave propagation at criticality.
main_problem: The study investigates the critical dynamics of a non-conserved order parameter, specifically analyzing the competition between propagating (relativistic) and overdamped (relaxational) behavior near criticality.
main_result: The paper shows that while both dynamic limits share static fixed points, they possess distinct dynamical scaling regimes; furthermore, the propagating regime is found to be unstable to any local equilibrium dissipation perturbation.
method: The analysis employs a supersymmetric field-theory formulation combined with two-loop Renormalization Group (RG) techniques applied near four spatial dimensions.
model_or_system: The system is a scalar field theory ($\phi(t, x)$) in thermal equilibrium whose dynamics are governed by an action incorporating both inertial and dissipative terms. The analysis compares the strictly overdamped limit to the dissipationless propagating limit.
key_observables: Dynamic critical exponent (z), static Gaussian and Wilson–Fisher fixed points, and the stability of the RG flow concerning local dissipation.
important_parameters: The ratio controlling local friction ($X$), the dimensionality ($d=4$), and the presence/absence of local equilibrium dissipation.
main_assumptions: The theory is assumed to be in thermal equilibrium, requiring adherence to the fluctuation–dissipation relation (KMS symmetry).
paper_structure: The paper systematically builds the supersymmetric structure, derives the effective action, analyzes static corrections, and then treats the overdamped and dissipationless limits separately before concluding with a comprehensive RG flow analysis.
why_interesting: The rigorous treatment of dynamic critical exponents and the stability analysis concerning dissipation provides deep insights into non-equilibrium dynamics relevant to phase transitions in many physical systems.

Figure 3: Local stability of the four fixed points on the mass-tuned critical surface. The propa- gating and overdamped boundaries lie at ρr = 0 and ρr = +∞, respectively. In the static direction, the Gaussian fixed points are repulsive and the Wilson–Fisher fixed points are attractive. In the dynamical direction, the propagating fixed points are repulsive and the overdamped fixed points are attractive. Consequently, the propagating Wilson–Fisher and overdamped Gaussian fixed points are saddles, while the overdamped Wilson–Fisher fixed point is the only fixed point attractive in both directions.
